literal: At the time, because Xiu had not sent Tanhe ahead and only beheaded him after Xi's defeat, he was charged with collusion and summoned to the Court of Justice.
idiomatic: Because he had not sent Tanhe up earlier and only killed him after Xi's fall, he was charged with collusion and haled to the Court of Justice.

literal: Vice Minister Cui Zhen exhausted the evidence and judged Xiu guilty of great treason.
idiomatic: Vice Minister Cui Zhen built the case and condemned him for treason.

literal: The Lu clan great and small were all seized.
idiomatic: Great and small of the Lu house were arrested.

literal: When an amnesty was due, he was first executed in prison.
idiomatic: An amnesty was coming; he was killed in prison first.

literal: Xiu's younger brother Kai still memorialized for justice; Emperor Xuanwu ordered Xiu's title restored and his son Jing to inherit falsely.
idiomatic: Brother Kai petitioned; Xuanwu restored Xiu's rank and let son Jing inherit.

literal: Kai, styled Zhijun, was careful, weighty, and fond of learning.
idiomatic: Kai, styled Zhijun, was careful and scholarly.

literal: He held the posts of Junior Tutor of the Heir Apparent and Attendant of the Yellow Gate.
idiomatic: He was Junior Tutor and Attendant of the Yellow Gate.

literal: Kai spent more than ten years at the pivot and was praised for loyalty.
idiomatic: More than ten years at court won him praise for loyalty.

literal: Later, when ill, he repeatedly memorialized begging to retire.
idiomatic: Illness drove him to beg retirement again and again.

literal: Made Administrator of Zhengping; seven years in the commandery, he was called a good official.
idiomatic: Made Administrator of Zhengping; seven years there made him a model magistrate.

literal: Earlier, when Emperor Xiaowen was about to discuss reforming old customs, the great ministers all looked troubled.
idiomatic: When Xiaowen planned to reform old ways, ministers looked troubled.

literal: He also often summoned Liu Fang, Guo Zuo, and others to plan with them and discuss government.
idiomatic: He often summoned Liu Fang, Guo Zuo, and others to plot policy.

literal: The imperial kin thought themselves now slighted and nursed resentment.
idiomatic: Imperial kin felt slighted and grew resentful.

literal: The emperor had Kai secretly explain to them: "His Majesty only wishes to broaden knowledge of former affairs and will simply ask about ancient forms.
idiomatic: The emperor had Kai tell them, "The throne only seeks to learn the old forms.

literal: He will never favor them and slight the old imperial kin."
idiomatic: He will not favor newcomers over kin."

literal: They then gradually relaxed.
idiomatic: Resentment eased.

literal: When brother Xiu fell into crime, Kai was also seized but escaped through amnesty.
idiomatic: When Xiu fell, Kai was seized but amnestied.

literal: Kai grieved his brother's death, wept without regard to season, nearly went blind, and pleaded injustice without end.
idiomatic: He mourned Xiu without cease, nearly blind, pleading injustice.

literal: By the beginning of Zhengshi, Xuanwu restored Xiu's office and title.
idiomatic: At Zhengshi's start Xuanwu restored Xiu's honors.

literal: Kai rejoiced greatly, set out wine, and gathered kin, saying: "These many years I bore illness and endured death for the clan's sake alone; now my wish is fulfilled."
idiomatic: Kai feasted his kin: "Years I clung to life for the house—now it is done."

literal: In that year he died; posthumously made General of Dragon Cavalry and Governor of Southern Qing, posthumous name Hui.
idiomatic: He died that year, posthumously Dragon Cavalry General and Governor of Southern Qing, posthumous name Hui.

literal: His eldest son Yong, styled Daohui, and his brother Gongzhi both had contemporary fame.
idiomatic: Eldest Yong, styled Daohui, and brother Gongzhi were famed.

literal: Luoyang Magistrate Jia Zhen saw the brothers and sighed: "I thought my old age done—yet I see a pair of jades again."
idiomatic: Magistrate Jia Zhen sighed, "I thought my age over—yet two jades shine again."

literal: Once the brothers together waited on Yellow Gate Attendant Sun Huiwei.
idiomatic: Once they waited together on Sun Huiwei of the Yellow Gate.

literal: He told the guests: "I did not expect the two Lus still in the corner.
idiomatic: He told guests, "The two Lus still grace the corner.

literal: My virtue falls short of Lord Zhang—I have no praise to offer."
idiomatic: I lack Zhang's grace to praise them."

literal: Yong held the posts of Right Master of the Household in the Ministry of Revenue and Gentleman of the Three Offices; dismissed for an offense.
idiomatic: Yong was Master of Revenue and Gentleman of the Three Offices, then dismissed.

literal: Later made General Who Subdues Waves.
idiomatic: Later General Who Subdues Waves.

literal: At death posthumously Champion General and Governor of Heng.
idiomatic: He died and was posthumously made Champion General and Governor of Heng.

literal: Yong modeled the Jijiu Pian as Wumeng Zhang, and Seven Enticements and Ten Drunkennesses—several dozen chapters of memorials.
idiomatic: Yong wrote Wumeng Zhang after Jijiu, plus Seven Enticements, Ten Drunkennesses, and dozens of memorials.

literal: Yong and Gongzhi in later years were not harmonious and were scorned by the age.
idiomatic: Late in life Yong and Gongzhi quarreled and were scorned.

literal: His son Yuan Gui held the post of Gentleman of the Masters of Writing.
idiomatic: Son Yuan Gui was a Masters of Writing gentleman.

literal: Yuan Gui's son Bo, versed in yin-yang and calendrics, held the post of Senior Clerk of Bingzhou.
idiomatic: Bo mastered yin-yang and calendars and was Senior Clerk of Bingzhou.

literal: Gongzhi, styled Jishun, had integrity and held the post of Governor of Eastern Jing.
idiomatic: Gongzhi, styled Jishun, was upright and Governor of Eastern Jing.

literal: Posthumously Minister of the Civil Service, posthumous name Yi.
idiomatic: Posthumously Minister of Civil Service, posthumous name Yi.

literal: Gongzhi's writings, poems, and fu totaled more than a thousand pieces.
idiomatic: His writings exceeded a thousand pieces.

literal: His son Ye, styled Renchong, devoted to letters; the preface to the Qi Code is Renchong's wording.
idiomatic: Son Ye, styled Renchong, wrote the preface to the Qi Code.

literal: He ended as Regular Attendant Direct and Unimpeded.
idiomatic: His last post was Regular Attendant Direct and Unimpeded.

literal: His younger brother Kuan, styled Renhui, was Junior Mentor of the Heir Apparent and attendant at the Forest of Literature.
idiomatic: Younger Kuan, styled Renhui, was Junior Mentor and Forest of Literature attendant.

literal: The Kuan brothers all had talent; critics called them the Three Martial.
idiomatic: The brothers were called the Three Martial.

literal: Xu's younger brother Gui held the posts of Eastern Palace Attendant and Commandant of the Imperial Transport.
idiomatic: Younger brother Gui was Eastern Palace Attendant and Transport Commandant.

literal: His son Zhen was Governor of Xia Province, posthumously Grand Master of the Imperial Stud, posthumous name Jing.
idiomatic: Son Zhen governed Xia, posthumously Grand Master of the Stud, posthumous name Jing.

literal: Zhen's son Xu was refined and quiet, fond of the Changes and apocryphal astrology; he compiled Essentials of the Five Stars and the True Chart of the Two Poles and grasped their essentials well.
idiomatic: Xu loved the Changes and omen lore, wrote on the Five Stars and the Two Poles, and mastered their core.

literal: In the Taihe era he was summoned as Erudite of the Secretariat and gradually promoted to Regular Attendant.
idiomatic: In Taihe he became Secretariat erudite, then Regular Attendant.

literal: Seeing the realm would fall into disorder, he hid on Mount Taihang and repeatedly refused summons.
idiomatic: Foreseeing chaos, he hid on Taihang and refused summons.

literal: After death he was posthumously made Governor of Bing, Fen, Heng, and Si.
idiomatic: After death he was posthumously governor of four provinces.

literal: His son Teng.
idiomatic: His son Teng.

literal: Teng, styled Xiansheng, from youth was bold and had great integrity.
idiomatic: Teng, styled Xiansheng, was bold and high-minded from youth.

literal: Following Erzhu Rong he pacified Ge Rong and for merit was enfeoffed Baron of Qinghe.
idiomatic: With Erzhu Rong he crushed Ge Rong and was made Baron of Qinghe.

literal: He was gradually promoted to Regular Attendant Direct and Unimpeded.
idiomatic: He rose to Regular Attendant Direct and Unimpeded.

literal: When Emperor Xiaowu moved west, he was on mission in Qingzhou and stayed at Ye as Administrator of Yangcheng.
idiomatic: When Xiaowu fled west, Teng was in Qingzhou and stayed at Ye as Yangcheng magistrate.

literal: In the ninth year of Datong the eastern army attacked Yangcheng and took him.
idiomatic: Datong 9 the eastern army took Yangcheng and captured him.

literal: Emperor Wen of Zhou released him and spoke with him; Teng discoursed at length on Eastern Province worthies and reviewed current affairs with rising and falling eloquence.
idiomatic: Zhou's Emperor Wen freed him; Teng praised eastern men and debated affairs with eloquence.

literal: Wen sighed: "You truly do not betray your roots!"
idiomatic: Wen sighed, "You have not betrayed your roots!"

literal: He was at once made Grand Commander within the Tent.
idiomatic: He was made Grand Commander within the Tent.

literal: Before long, Junior Tutor of the Heir Apparent, then Martial Guard General.
idiomatic: Soon Junior Tutor, then Martial Guard General.

literal: Once known to Wen, Teng wished to win merit abroad and did not want inner posts.
idiomatic: Known to Wen, he wanted frontier merit, not palace posts.

literal: When the Ankang bandit Huang Zhongbao and others rebelled and besieged Eastern Liangzhou,
idiomatic: When Huang Zhongbao besieged Eastern Liangzhou,

literal: provisions in the city were exhausted; an edict ordered Teng to lead troops and smash them.
idiomatic: stores ran out; Teng was sent and broke the siege.

literal: When the army returned, he was made Governor of Long.
idiomatic: On return he was Governor of Long.

literal: He was sent to open the Tongjiang route straight to Southern Qin.
idiomatic: He opened the Tongjiang road to Southern Qin.

literal: Wen told him: "This is the day you earn your pillar rank."
idiomatic: Wen said, "Today you earn pillar rank."

literal: He at once removed his own gold belt and gave it to him.
idiomatic: He gave Teng his own gold belt.

literal: The provincials Li Guangsi and Li Wu held rugged passes; successive administrations could not control them.
idiomatic: Li Guangsi and Li Wu held the mountains; no governor broke them.

literal: Teng secretly had many scaling ladders made and by night stormed and broke them, seizing Guangsi and the rest below the drum.
idiomatic: Teng built ladders, struck by night, and seized them at the drum.

literal: Their party had Ren Gongxin, who besieged the prefectural city and asked that Guangsi and Wu be spared to disperse the troops and beg pardon.
idiomatic: Ren Gongxin besieged the city and begged mercy for Guangsi and Wu.

literal: Teng told the soldiers: "If I do not kill Guangsi and the rest, I may be said to waste the army's gain and grow the foe."
idiomatic: Teng said, "Spare them and I waste victory and feed the enemy."

literal: He then beheaded Guangsi and Wu and displayed the heads.
idiomatic: He beheaded both and showed the heads.

literal: He then led troops in fierce attack and captured them all.
idiomatic: Then he charged and took all.

literal: Promoted to General of Agile Cavalry, Commissioner with credentials equal to the Three Excellencies, transferred to Governor of Jiang, advanced to Duke of Shangyong.
idiomatic: He rose to Agile Cavalry General and Commissioner, became Governor of Jiang, Duke of Shangyong.

literal: The Mulong Liao of Lingzhou relied on terrain; they constantly raided.
idiomatic: Lingzhou's Mulong Liao raided from the hills.

literal: The Liao made mountains their walls; assault could not take them.
idiomatic: They walled the mountains; assault failed.

literal: Teng then set up much music and miscellaneous entertainments below the walls to show no will to fight.
idiomatic: He staged music and shows below the walls, feigning peace.

literal: The bandits indeed cast aside arms; some brought wives and children to watch from the walls.
idiomatic: They dropped weapons and brought families to watch.

literal: Teng knew them unprepared and loosed troops to strike; all were killed or broken.
idiomatic: Seeing them slack, he attacked and destroyed them.

literal: At the beginning of Emperor Ming of Zhou, the Yi and Xia of eight provinces of Ling and Mei all rebelled and stormed commanderies and counties; Teng led troops and pacified them.
idiomatic: Ming of Zhou's start saw eight provinces rebel; Teng pacified them.

literal: When Duke of Qi Xian was stationed in Shu, Teng was made Governor of Long and all troops Xian brought into Shu for defense were entrusted to Teng's command.
idiomatic: Duke Xian of Qi in Shu made Teng Governor of Long and gave him all garrison troops.

literal: Duke Zhao came to replace Xian and again asked to keep Teng.
idiomatic: Duke Zhao replaced Xian and kept Teng.

literal: Moved to Area Commander of Long, concurrently Governor.
idiomatic: He became Area Commander of Long, still governor.

literal: In the second year of Baoding, the Shiban people of Zizhou rebelled, killed the commandery administrator, held the passes, and provincial troops could not control them.
idiomatic: Baoding 2, Zizhou's Shiban rebels killed the magistrate and held the hills.

literal: Teng led troops to strike and broke and beheaded them all.
idiomatic: Teng crushed and beheaded them.

literal: Then southern barbarians rebelled everywhere along the mountain roads, hard to surprise.
idiomatic: Then hill barbarians rose on every road.

literal: He therefore measured terrain and opened roads as needed.
idiomatic: He surveyed terrain and cut roads where needed.

literal: The Liao feared his might and came to submit on the wind.
idiomatic: Barbarians submitted to his awe.

literal: Roads he opened often bore ancient inscriptions—old tracks of Zhuge Liang and Huan Wen.
idiomatic: His roads uncovered inscriptions—tracks of Zhuge Liang and Huan Wen.

literal: That year, Tieshan Liao cut the inner Jiang route so couriers could not pass.
idiomatic: That year Tieshan Liao cut the inner river courier route.

literal: Teng advanced to attack; in one day he took three walled places and received thirty thousand who surrendered.
idiomatic: Teng marched, took three forts in a day, and won thirty thousand submits.

literal: The emperor, because Teng's mother was in Qi, did not yet order an eastern campaign.
idiomatic: His mother was in Qi, so the throne held the eastern campaign.

literal: When a kinsman returned from Qi to court, Duke of Jin Hu memorialized to tell Teng: "Qi has already executed your mother and elder brother."
idiomatic: A kinsman from Qi reported, "Qi killed your mother and brother."

literal: It was meant to stir his rage.
idiomatic: The aim was to stir his rage.

literal: Teng then mourned with blood and tears, his will set on revenge.
idiomatic: Teng mourned with blood and vowed revenge.

literal: In the fourth year, Duke Xian of Qi and Duke Hu of Jin campaigned east and asked Teng as deputy.
idiomatic: Year 4, Qi and Jin marched east and named Teng deputy.

literal: Duke Zhao was then in Shu and again wished to keep him.
idiomatic: Duke Zhao in Shu again tried to keep him.

literal: Duke Hu wrote to Zhao; Teng was ordered to ride post-horses back to court and assist Xian in the eastern attack.
idiomatic: Hu wrote Zhao; Teng raced back to join the eastern attack.

literal: At the beginning of Tianhe, the Man and Dan of Xin Province held the river gorges and rebelled for more than two thousand li; again Teng was ordered to attack.
idiomatic: Tianhe's start saw Xin Man and Dan hold gorges for two thousand li; Teng was sent.

literal: Teng went down the river; when the army reached Tangkou he divided forces and struck; wherever he went, he broke them.
idiomatic: He sailed downriver to Tangkou, split forces, and swept all before him.

literal: He then built a victory mound to display martial achievement.
idiomatic: He raised a victory mound.

literal: Fuling Commandery Administrator Lan Xiuzu again raised troops in revolt over two thousand li.
idiomatic: Fuling's Lan Xiuzu rebelled across two thousand li.

literal: Again Teng was ordered to attack; Ba and Shu were all settled, and an edict ordered a stele to record his merit.
idiomatic: Teng was sent again; Ba-Shu was settled and a stele ordered.

literal: From Longzhou until then, Teng had repeatedly broken and pacified the various bandits; in rewards he received eight hundred slaves and concubines and horses and cattle in proportion.
idiomatic: From Longzhou on he had broken every bandit; rewards were eight hundred slaves and herds in proportion.
